meta.title: Marc Andreessen on how the internet changed news, politics, and outrage | The a16z Show
meta.speakers: Marc Andreessen; host of Monitoring the Situation (a16z)
meta.thread_line: 5 threads · CNN's 'Randomonium' reborn online · the 2.5-day outrage cycle · the past was more violent · ops & availability cascades · legacy media's collapse and the first internet president

snapshot: Marc Andreessen's opening conversation on day one of **Monitoring the Situation**, an a16z-backed live show, ~66 min, on how the internet reshaped news and outrage.
CNN's founding idea, 'Randomonium' (lock onto the current thing and cover it nonstop), has been reinvented by X and live streaming.
Updating McLuhan: 'if it's on the internet, it's a viral social media meme'. Each outrage spikes and decays over ~2.5 days, then a new one replaces it.
Contrarian core: political violence is at an all-time low. Online 'virtual combat' absorbs rage that past media (posters, radio, TV) turned into street violence.
The 1990-2014 era of centralized media was 'suppressed volatility'. The Ben Franklin era of 15 papers per city and sock-puppet alts was the historical norm.
Ops are real, and paid moral-issue influence is legal and undisclosed. Andreessen says much AI doomerism is 'bought and paid for', yet ops only work if they resonate.
Legacy media is collapsing, but a 'barbell' of short-form video and 3-10 hour podcasts is growing. His guess for the first true internet president is 2032.

themes.title: CNN's 'Randomonium' became the internet: lock onto the current thing and never let go
themes.lead: CNN's original plan of wall-to-wall coverage of whatever is most transfixing right now is exactly what social media now does, amplified by McLuhan's two laws.
bullets: Source: the little-read book *Me and Ted Against the World* by **Reese Schonfeld**, the lawyer who wired Ted Turner's first satellite deal. In ~1981 they pitched 24-hour news. Turner wanted 15 hours, assuming nobody watched overnight.
Schonfeld's 'Randomonium': at any moment there's one transfixing 'current thing'. Cover it continuously, put whatever fragments you get on air, and apologize later if wrong.

The breakthrough was the **1991 Gulf War**, with live coverage from Baghdad. CNN spent 20 years chasing a repeat (Lewinsky, OJ) and then became 'something completely different'. The internet (X, YouTube, Twitch) reinvented Randomonium.

McLuhan's **global village**, which he meant as an observation rather than praise: media turns the world into a small town with no privacy. Humans can manage a Dunbar number of ~150 relationships, and the internet hands you 8 billion 'up in your grill'.

McLuhan's 'if it's on television, it's a television show': events get squeezed into sitcoms and dramas that end in a moral lesson. *Seinfeld*'s rule, 'no learning, no hugging', stood out because it broke that format.

The internet version: 'if it's on the internet, it's a viral social media meme'. Even an alien invasion would become a meme, then a moral panic and a hunt for scapegoats. Thought experiment: Pearl Harbor in 1941 with Twitter.

quote.text: If it's on the internet, it's a viral social media meme.

names.name: CNN
names.blurb: Founded on Reese Schonfeld's 'Randomonium'; peaked with the 1991 Gulf War; now 'completely different'.

themes.title: Every outrage lasts ~2.5 days, and its truth and scale don't matter
themes.lead: A current thing needs outrage, two tribes and an underlying moral fight. Whether it happened, or how many people it hurt, barely changes the reaction.
bullets: Each viral explosion spikes and then decays with a half-life of about **2.5 days**. It's never resolved, only replaced, and a week later nobody remembers it.
That's why Andreessen says politics can't be predicted: from April 20 to the November midterms there are 100-120 cycles, so the vote turns on the economy and whatever meme is live that day.

The recipe: activate outrage ('the news is called the news, not the importance'). Think wrestling for men, *Real Housewives* for women, *The Apprentice* in between. Add *West Side Story* tribes that attack values, then dox each other and try to get each other fired.

Truth doesn't matter, and ambiguity helps because it's easier to argue about. Scale doesn't matter either: one victim can outrage more than 10,000 (Stalin: 'a single death is a tragedy'). Orwell on the Spanish Civil War said the same about atrocities (nuns killed, later My Lai).
Jussie Smollett as a case study, now echoed in a Keanu Reeves Apple TV film where Jonah Hill's crisis lawyer staged the attack. The host adds the 'Astronomer CEO/HR' episode as a lighter example.

Viral videos start midway. The first one that mattered, **Rodney King**, began with the beating, and the Central Park birdwatcher clip showed no run-up. People only pull out phones once it's interesting, and trial evidence arrives a year later.
René Girard: scapegoating works because people forget it's a cycle. Cancellation hit people for things they 'literally never did'.

quote.text: The news is called the news, not the importance.

themes.watch: Andreessen stresses he's describing the mechanism, not endorsing it: 'I'm not saying I think this is all good.' His advice is to keep part of your brain aware that you're being slotted into a tribe.

themes.title: Online rage is a safety valve: political violence is at an all-time low, and calm centralized media was the anomaly
themes.lead: Andreessen argues every earlier medium fed physical violence, the past was far more violent than we remember, and 1990-2014 was an artificial lull.
bullets: Media and violence: posters drove the Spanish Civil War (the test bed for communism and Nazism), radio was the Nazi regime's medium (and FDR's), and TV fueled Vietnam and the riots of the '60s and '70s.
His 'moral defense' of social media is that virtual combat absorbs rage: 'if you're sitting at home scrolling social media getting mad, at least you're not out in the street hurting people.'

The past was worse than remembered. *All in the Family* (Norman Lear, Carroll O'Connor's Archie Bunker vs Rob Reiner's 'Meathead') and *Family Ties* (Michael J. Fox as Alex P. Keaton) both backfired as their conservative foils became the stars.

Going back: the 101st Airborne desegregating schools, the Red Scare, the World Wars, the Depression, the Civil War, the Napoleonic Wars and Gutenberg-era violence. Duels were normal for powerful men, and labor strikes met machine guns.
On depression: the rise tracks countries with benefits or school accommodations for diagnoses, which he calls a 'statistical artifact'. He concedes things have felt wilder since ~2014.
Centralized media peaked around 1970 (one paper per city, three networks, three newsmagazines, two wire services), creating **suppressed volatility** from the Cold War's end to ~2014.

The norm was fragmentation: 10-15 papers per city in the Revolution era. Ben Franklin started a paper to keep his press busy and ran ~15 pseudonymous 'alts' arguing with each other. The 1800 Jefferson-Adams election's slander 'is way beyond' today's.

quote.text: The fact that political violence is at like an all-time low in Western society is something that people really don't talk about.

themes.watch: The depression-data claim and the all-time-low violence claim are Andreessen's reading ('I don't even concede the premise'), stated without citing a specific dataset.

themes.status: PAID MORAL-ISSUE INFLUENCE IS LEGAL AND UNDISCLOSED
themes.title: Ops are everywhere, but calling something 'just an op' is cope
themes.lead: Movements often start as deliberate availability cascades, yet an op only matters if it resonates, and many become real.
bullets: Timur Kuran (preference falsification) and Cass Sunstein name the viral outrage cycle an **availability cascade**, and trace each one to an 'availability entrepreneur' who picks the specific victim or issue to focus on.
His example is Rosa Parks, a trained activist rather than a random passenger. 'It started as an op', but it unlocked profoundly positive change, so how it started is 'a footnote'.

His Machiavellian thought experiment: with a black budget, paid influencers and a bot army, the goal isn't paid posts forever but getting people to actually believe it, so ops aim to become organic. Real movements mix organic and staged parts, and 'that's just an op' is cope when the outcome is real.
The regulatory gap: paid shampoo influencers must disclose, and political donations are disclosed, but paying influencers to push a **moral or political position** is legal 'in the dark'.

AI policy: 'a lot of the AI doomers… is basically bought and paid for'. His example is a just-announced free 'influencer camp' fellowship for doomers, funded by MIRI 'and other donors'. 'Is it a conspiracy if it's in plain sight?'

Bot farms exist, and an influencer can have a bot army behind them without knowing it. Andreessen admits there are 'probably more ops than I've been willing to acknowledge', but they only work if the cause already resonates.
The host's lens is 'emergent collusion': aligned incentives look coordinated. Since joining a16z, people have attributed things to them that they aren't doing.

quote.text: Just because things start as ops doesn't mean they're not real.

themes.watch: a16z is a combatant in the AI policy fight ('we're deep into this'), so the 'doomers are paid' charge comes from the opposing side. The Rosa Parks framing ('started as an op') is his own characterization.

names.name: MIRI
names.blurb: Andreessen: funds a new free influencer fellowship for AI doomers 'and other donors', an example of dark-money moral influence.

themes.title: Legacy media is collapsing into private equity, the barbell is rising, and the first true internet president is still ahead
themes.lead: Trust and ratings for centralized media are in free fall, while short-form video and marathon podcasts both grow. Trump is a hybrid, and the pure internet candidate is coming.
bullets: Trust in centralized institutions has been falling since ~1970 ('WTF happened in 1971', 55 years) and hits record lows every survey. Cable news, newspapers and magazines are in 'full scale collapse', and non-adapters get 'run by private equity'.

Adapters: the **New York Times** has adapted, CBS acquired the Free Press, and Mark Halperin is the rare legacy-to-new-media bridge (his Trump Bible-verses interview). MTS mixes him with 21-year-old Twitch streamer Theo.
The barbell: short-form video (TikTok, Instagram Reels, X) on one end, 3-hour podcasts on the other. Lex Fridman runs up to 7 hours, Balaji did 10, and Rogan and Lex see high completion rates.
The rise of substance includes Substack, long-form essays on X, online courses and AI **deep research** in ChatGPT and Claude that writes '30 pages… basically a textbook'.
Practitioner media means people who do the thing explain it, like Andrej Karpathy on AI. Andreessen grew up on Charlie Rose at midnight and needed a DVR.

Deepfakes aren't new: he cites the Gulf of Tonkin ('a fish') and says Russiagate turned out to be 'quite an elaborate fake'. In 1960, Kennedy-Nixon radio listeners and TV viewers picked different winners.

Internet elections so far: 2008 (Obama fundraising), 2016 (Trump's social media), 2024 (podcasts). Trump is a hybrid who reads TV chyrons on mute and tweets to change the current thing. A 100% online president who ignores TV is coming, 'probably… 32'.

quote.text: There will be an internet president who gets elected… entirely based on the internet.

themes.watch: a16z backs Monitoring the Situation, so the 'new media is winning' thesis is partly a pitch for the show hosting the conversation. The 2032 date is a guess ('I don't know when').

names.name: New York Times (NYT)
names.blurb: Legacy outlet that adapted well to the new media world, per the host and Andreessen.

takeaways.title: Wait 2.5 days before forming a strong view on a viral outrage; the cycle usually ends before the facts arrive.
Ask 'what happened before the video started?' before sharing any viral clip.
Notice when you're being sorted into a moral tribe, and keep part of your brain on the objective facts.
Check who funds a moral or policy campaign; paid issue influence doesn't have to be disclosed.
Lean into the substance end of the barbell: long-form podcasts, practitioner media and AI deep-research reports.

claims.claim: The first true internet president, elected without caring about TV, arrives around 2032.
The November midterms will turn on the economy and the viral meme of that day, not today's issues, after ~100-120 outrage cycles.
Legacy media properties that don't adapt end up run by private equity.

glossary.def: Reese Schonfeld's founding CNN concept: lock onto the single most transfixing current event and cover it nonstop.
McLuhan's idea that electronic media turns the world into one small town with no privacy.
The ~150 stable relationships a human can maintain.
Kuran and Sunstein's term for a belief gaining momentum because repetition makes it more mentally available.
The person who deliberately picks the specific story or victim that kicks off an availability cascade.
Timur Kuran's term for people publicly stating views they don't privately hold.
Andreessen's label for ~1990-2014, when centralized media muted political conflict.
The text crawl at the bottom of a TV news screen.
